1:
The title is taken three ways before anything else is settled. John Gill makes it a prophecy concerning Babylon, noting that the Greek and Arabic render the word vision, and that it signifies taking up a speech against a place. Matthew Henry hears the other sense: a burden is a lesson they would be loath to learn, and those who will not make the word of God their rest will find it made a burden to them. John Wesley says the title is commonly given to sad prophecies, grievous burdens to those on whom they are laid.

Where the oracle sits is explained structurally. Charles Ellicott notes that the title recurs over six later chapters and marks off a collection of utterances on the future of surrounding nations. John Calvin explains why such a collection was needed: when great changes take place, some think God sports with human affairs and others that everything is driven by the blind violence of fortune, and few are aware that these things are appointed by his purpose; there is nothing, he adds, of which it is harder to convince men than that providence governs the world.

Whether the prophecy is genuinely a prophecy is raised and answered by Ellicott. Its authenticity has been questioned, he says, partly on style and partly because it anticipates Babylon's destruction with a distinctness implying a prophecy written after the event; the first objection rests on no sufficient evidence, and the second implies a view of prophecy that excludes divinely given foreknowledge, which he does not accept. Adam Clarke assumes what Ellicott argues, taking this and the next chapter as one prophecy of Babylon's fall to the Medes and Persians, delivered two hundred years before the event. Delitzsch supplies a stylistic argument on the same side, that one word here is peculiarly this prophet's and its combination with another so unusual that one could hardly expect it in two unrelated authors.

The mountain the banner stands on is disputed. Gill offers a high mountain in Media or Persia, or else Babylon itself, called a mountain not for its situation, since it lay on a plain, but for its eminence. Calvin reports that reading but thinks it better taken indefinitely, of a signal drawing a vast assembly from distant countries. Ellicott and Delitzsch agree that the mountain is a bare one, where no trees would hide the standard. Delitzsch counts a threefold signal, the banner on a bald mountain, the voice raised high, and the shaking of the hand, all favourites with this prophet. Ellicott adds that the same words were used earlier of Israel's invaders and here of its avengers, and that the shaking of the hand is the gesture of generals pointing at the city to be destroyed.

Wesley thinks the prophet intimates that the enemy would come out of the mountainous country of Media. Clarke removes a word from the verse as useless, omitted by an ancient manuscript and the Latin.

Who the sanctified ones are is agreed, though the reason differs. Gill says the Medes and Persians are so called not because sanctified by the Spirit but because set apart in God's counsel for a special work, the command reaching them by a secret instinct. Clarke says nothing is plainer than that the verb means to consecrate or appoint to a purpose, and adopts a bishop's rendering, my enrolled warriors. Ellicott notes the word is applied even to fierce tribes as appointed for that work, just as a later chapter calls Cyrus the anointed of the Lord, and that the phrase about rejoicing denotes the invaders' proud sense of doing God's work. Delitzsch has them rejoicing with the pride of men intoxicated by victory. Calvin raises the oddity nobody else notices, that a private man here commands the Medes and Persians, which he could not do unless God had fortified him.
4:
The gathering army is placed geographically by some and rhetorically by others. John Calvin explains the manner: the prophets are not satisfied with speaking unless they give a bold picture, since plain words do not strike us so powerfully as figures delineating a living resemblance. John Gill hears the noise on the mountains of Media or on those bordering Chaldea. Charles Ellicott has the prophet hear the tramp of forces mustering on the mountains north of Babylonia, adding candidly that his geography was probably vague. Keil and Delitzsch note only how fast the command is executed, the great army already coming down from the hills. Adam Clarke supplies its composition from another prophet, who calls it an assembly of great nations from the north country and names three kingdoms with the Median kings.

The phrase about the end of heaven is read three ways. Gill takes it for the east, on a rabbi's authority, and notes that the old paraphrase has the ends of the earth, which suits Persia and Media, since between them and Babylon lay all Assyria. Clarke cites the same rabbi, and reports one word missing from a manuscript and the Syriac. Ellicott reads it as cosmology, representing an age in which the earth was an extended plain with the sky rising like a vault above, so the phrase stands for the furthest limit of discovery. John Wesley says the words are not to be understood strictly.

Calvin uses the same verse for providence: the operations of war do not spring up at random, for though everything disorderly is vomited out by the passions of men, God rules on high, and armed men are nothing but his instruments; they come from far because we fear no danger until it is close, Babylon being so fortified that there seemed no way in. Wesley makes the same point, that the Medes and Persians were only a rod in God's hand.

The howling is addressed to men who had no intention of howling. Gill has the Babylonians called to lament instead of feasting as they were the night the city fell, and observes that though some two hundred and fifty years lay between prophecy and event, it is represented as at hand to show its certainty. Calvin says the prophet does not really instruct them, as if he hoped it would profit, but uses direct address for emphasis; the day is so called because when the Lord delays judgment he seems to cease from his office, like a judge who does not ascend the bench. Matthew Henry calls the passage a very elegant and lively description of the confusion to come, God being about to appear in wrath.

Ellicott handles the same verse as language: it almost verbally reproduces a line in an earlier prophet, and the phrase for destruction from the Almighty carries the emphasis of assonance and perhaps of etymology, since many derive the divine name from the verb to destroy, so destruction from the destroyer would be a fair equivalent.

The terror that follows is described physically, and one detail puzzles them. Ellicott finds the image of powerless agony in prophets earlier and later, and its most striking parallel in a psalm probably contemporary with this chapter; on the faces like flames he grants the comparison seems at first to describe those who cause terror rather than those who feel it, but says what is meant is the moment when ordinary pallor flashes into intensity and the eyeballs glare. Wesley takes the words for faces inflamed with rage and torment, and has them amazed to see so impregnable a city taken so easily. Calvin turns it into a taunt: the cruelty that boiled in Babylonian hearts is ridiculed indirectly, since it lies with God to enfeeble them until their courage falls at once, and when the heart quakes fortifications are of no use.
9:
The day is announced as already arrived. John Gill notes the verb may be rendered is come, the event at hand but set out as past, and John Wesley finds words heaped together to signify extremity of anger. John Calvin raises the question the others do not: why should the day be called terrible, when nothing is more desirable than to have God present? Because one must consider who is addressed: the prophets describe God according to the diversity of the hearers, merciful to the merciful and severe to the ungodly, so the slightest mention of him fills wicked men with terror.

Whether the darkened heavens are literal is disputed. Gill is explicit that what follows is not literal but figurative, expressive of a dispensation with no light, comfort, or hope. Charles Ellicott agrees that the words in their first application had a figurative and not a literal fulfilment, such imagery being the natural symbolism of terror. Yet Gill later reports that some think the shaking was literally fulfilled at the taking of the city, with thunders and lightnings and the lights withheld.

Adam Clarke supplies the poetics: Hebrew poets express prosperity by images from nature's most striking parts, the moon like the meridian sun and the sun's light augmented sevenfold; destruction by the opposite images, the stars obscured, the moon withdrawing her light, the earth quaking, all tending toward their original chaos. Calvin reaches the same place differently: the prophets add extravagant modes of speaking that place God's anger before our eyes, and yet do not go beyond what took place, since no image is so alarming that the reality is not more terrible.

Ellicott identifies the constellation: the noun means foolhardy or impious and is rendered Orion elsewhere, and points to a widely diffused legend, since the Persian name for it is Nimrod and the Arabian Giant, while in Greek myth Orion is a giant hunter slain by Zeus for outrage against the gods.

That the world means Babylon is agreed by all. Gill takes it for the kingdom of Babylon, so called for its extent and population, as the Roman empire is called the whole world, leaving open whether the evil visited is sin or punishment. Clarke gives classical parallels: the Greek word used of the Roman empire and of Judea, and Minos calling Crete his world. Calvin adds that Babylon seemed to occupy nearly the whole earth, yet nothing is so lofty that God cannot seize it with one finger; its crimes are named so that no one may think God delights in afflictions.

What makes a man more precious than gold divides them. Gill offers three readings: the scarcity of men after slaughter, the Medes' resolve to spare none however much gold was offered, or the fear keeping men from taking arms for pay. Clarke has the conquerors accept no ransom for poor man or honourable, all falling by the sword or going captive. Ellicott hears in both words for man the frailty of his nature, and notes the gold of Ophir was proverbial. Calvin, describing the savagery, concedes that history gives a different account, and that Daniel, an eye-witness, relates otherwise.

The shaking is read grammatically and typologically. Keil and Delitzsch hear God revealing his purpose, a visitation punishing the wicked and humbling the proud, and take the two prefixes as causative: because wrath falls upon men, every creature not itself the object of judgment becomes a medium of it. Ellicott finds the same terms used later of the great day, carried beyond Babylon to every world-power resisting the righteousness of God. Calvin says the pictures console the godly, who are distressed when it is well with the wicked, and undeceive men who think their roots too deep to be pulled up. Wesley calls it a poetical description of horrors, as if heaven and earth were to meet.
14:
The verse opens with a subject nobody can find. Adam Clarke says there is plainly a defect in the sentence, the subject of the proposition being lost: what is it that shall be like a chased roe? The Greek happily supplies the remnant, a manuscript the inhabitant, which makes a tolerably good sense, though he much prefers the Greek. John Gill reports the same variants without deciding, the Syriac reading they shall be, the Greek and Arabic they that are left, and adds a rabbi's view that the fugitives are foreigners who happened to be in Babylon.

The three who name the fugitives agree. Keil and Delitzsch call Babylon the market of the world in central Asia, a rendezvous for the most diverse nations, now scattered in wildest flight, and quote a Greek tragedian's phrase for such a mixed multitude. Charles Ellicott cites the same line, adding that some would return to their own lands though without a leader. John Calvin makes it military: auxiliary and hired troops will be of no avail, timorous as roes and scattered as sheep, keeping neither their ranks nor any order. John Wesley says these were soldiers of other nations whom she had hired.

Two classes of the doomed are distinguished. Delitzsch takes the first phrase of those seized in the city by the invaders and the second of those overtaken in flight; Ellicott divides it identically. Clarke presses that none escape, neither those who flee singly nor those who retreat in compact bodies, and prefers a Greek manuscript variant as properly expressive of the Hebrew. Calvin notes a rival rendering that refers the second clause to old men already worn out with age, but keeps his own, and brings in the historian's report that by Cyrus's command they slew everyone met at nightfall and next day all who had not laid down arms.

On the infants the reading is moral rather than textual. Gill sees retaliation for what Babylon had done to the Jews, and takes the phrase before their eyes to govern the following clauses too. Ellicott hears the verse behind the dread beatitude the exiles pronounced on the ministers of a righteous vengeance, and observes that such outrages were then, as ever since, the inevitable accompaniments of a city's capture. Calvin calls it the utmost pitch of ferocity, the more shocking for being done before the parents, and the mark of enemies who wish the very name of the subdued rooted out.

Naming the conquerors is where the chapter's apologetic weight falls. Gill says this at last explains who the sanctified ones were, and that the Persians are included though only the Medes are named, since Cyrus served under the king of Media; that they are named some hundreds of years before the event he treats as a strong proof of the truth of prophecy. Calvin argues the same from the other side: no jealousy existed between the two peoples, and the Medes then had no power to harm Babylon, so no human conjecture could have reached it. Ellicott turns ethnographer, making the Medes a mixed people of Aryan conquerors over an earlier race, unlike the pure Iranian Persians.

Gold and bows close the passage. Clarke explains that no ransom will buy a life, and cites the epic scenes in which the vanquished appeal to the pity and avarice of the victor; Wesley says the indifference is comparative, the Medes pursuing destruction more eagerly than spoil. Delitzsch insists the bows do not stand for the bowmen, the arrows doing the dashing. Clarke reports that the Persians used bows three cubits long, and with a metal bow of that length a soldier might dash as well as shoot. Calvin rejects the reading that has the children used in place of arrows, and concedes that we do not read the Medes were so cruel, the city flourishing long afterwards.
19:
Two find the same pun independently. John Gill notes that the word rendered glory is the one rendered roe a few verses earlier, so that Babylon was once a pleasant roe and is now a chased one; Matthew Henry says the same, adding the titles head of gold and lady of kingdoms. Keil and Delitzsch read the epithets historically: ornament of kingdoms because the city was the centre of many conquered kingdoms now avenging themselves upon it, and the pride of the Chaldeans because it was the old dwelling-place of the lowlanders, a people related to the mountain tribes of the north-east though of other origin and manners.

Its grandeur is documented, not asserted. Charles Ellicott says the words paint the impression the city made on all who saw it, and gathers witnesses: the king who exulted in a city he claimed to have built though his work was mainly restoration, the Greek historian who called it the strongest of Assyria's cities, adorned beyond any his eyes had seen, and the tragedian's epithet of gold-abounding Babylon. Adam Clarke measures instead: on the lowest ancient account a square forty-five miles round, walls two hundred feet high and fifty broad, a hundred brass gates.

The comparison with the cities of the plain, Ellicott observes, had clearly become proverbial. Henry grants the difference and keeps the force: the ruin was not so miraculous or sudden, but as effectual, though gradual. John Calvin explains why the prophets speak so, leaving no room for the compassion by which men relieve their minds, whereas the godly under chastisement keep the hope that God will not altogether destroy them; hence we ought not judge by outward appearance, since we often think the children of God ruined when their salvation is at hand.

The desolation is tested against report. Gill cites a traveller of Hadrian's time who said the greatest city the sun ever saw had nothing left but a wall, what now bears the name being a new city on another site. Calvin takes the verb for continuance, so there is no hope of restoring the place, and finds the sharpest proof in the Arab: the site must be marvellously forsaken to be disregarded by a wandering people who had left a barren country to feed flocks and hunt. Ellicott confirms a literal fulfilment, the Bedouin shrinking from the ruins from desolation and superstitious horror.

Nobody can name the animals, and two admit it. Gill lists what the versions and rabbis offer: for the first creature, monstrous things, apes, martens or sables of the weasel kind, and a word close to the Arabic for wild cats; for the next, sirens, hyenas, onocentaurs and owls. Calvin says outright that he cannot tell how to translate, given the diversity of translators, since the use of these things did not continue and the Jews have not retained the knowledge; whether it is quadruped or bird he thinks of little importance. Ellicott reads the terms generically, the groaners probably horned owls and the screamers ostriches, and the shaggy ones goats, or a grotesque like the Greek goat-god, or most probably a baboon. Wesley says only that the learned agree they are frightful and solitary.

The last verse is corrected, then dated. Clarke calls the received word for palaces a plain mistake, corrected in two manuscripts and three versions, and reaches for the Persian couplet in which the spider holds the veil in Caesar's palace and the owl stands sentinel on the watch-tower. Ellicott finds a false etymology under the received rendering, the word strictly meaning wailers, its form probably imitating a beast's cry, while desolate houses is literally among their widows, a word closely resembling that for castles. Calvin faces the delay: the city was not so speedily overturned, and the shortness of the time is asserted because the beginnings were soon seen.
